As Woodside continues operating within the ASX 20, growing attention is also being directed towards ASX Oil and Gas Stocks as companies across the sector navigate changing market conditions.
For readers following WDS ASX news today, its energy projects remain firmly in focus.

Scarborough is a gas development in the Carnarvon Basin that connects offshore wells to a floating production unit and then to onshore facilities for processing and liquefaction. The company's October report described the overall project as very close to complete, a stage at which the focus moves from construction to commissioning and start-up.

Commissioning is the process of testing each system, from pipes and valves to control software, before gas flows. It is methodical and often uneventful, but it can be sensitive to schedule because every system must be signed off in sequence. That is why a pause of even a short duration draws attention, and why the resumption of work was noted. Floating production units are designed to stay at sea for years, processing gas near the wells and sending it to shore by pipeline, which reduces the amount of infrastructure needed on the seabed.

Woodside Energy (ASX:WDS) Energy Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX:WDS) 30.91 AUD +0.010 0.032% Last Updated at: 2026-11-12T05:55:00Z is facing fresh questions today over how its giant Browse gas project off the Kimberley coast would be financed, after an advocacy group argued that tightening bank lending policies are shrinking the pool of capital available for new fossil fuel developments. The report, published on Thursday, lands as crude prices climb again and as Asian energy importers place a growing premium on reliable long-term gas supply.

There is a debate, but not yet a squeeze. Critics say Browse could struggle to borrow the very large sums it would need, pointing to lenders that have stepped back from new upstream oil and gas projects. Woodside's response is that the project is still at the design stage, that no financing decisions have been made, and that those decisions ultimately rest with lenders.
Market commentary quoted in the coverage also pushed back, arguing that local bank appetite is a minor factor for a joint venture with access to international debt markets.

sum: The Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX: WDS) share price has seen its fair share of volatility this year. After dropping 8% in November to date, it's a good time to ask if the ASX energy share is a buy.
As the above chart shows, the business is lower than it has been for months, so brave investors may be wondering what experts think of the company after its recent capital markets update.
Let's look at a couple of highlights of what Woodside said on 5 November 2026.
Woodside outlined a clear plan to further improve its operational and project execution, as well as maximising value from its global LNG-led portfolio.
It noted that it's targeting a portfolio return on average capital employed of between 12% and 15% by the mid-2030s.

In terms of the dividend, Woodside announced a new distribution policy of between 20% and 40% of adjusted operating cash flows. The company said it will prioritise 20% of adjusted operating cash flow as a base dividend, with up to another 20% available for additional dividends and/or share buybacks.
It also announced a new capital framework, meaning the economics of spending money on growth must be more compelling than paying additional capital to shareholders.

sum: - A US congressional vote lands in the same week as the Melbourne Cup and an RBA decision, giving Australian markets an unusually crowded calendar.
- Energy names, companies reporting in US dollars, and locally listed funds tracking American benchmarks sit closest to the outcome.
- Political gridlock in Washington tends to narrow the range of policy surprises, something equity markets have historically digested calmly.

Australians will spend this week watching three very different races at once: a horse race in Melbourne, a cash rate call from the Reserve Bank, and a US congressional contest that rarely makes the front page here but quietly shapes earnings across the ASX 200. The outcome will decide which party controls Congress, and with it the direction of legislation, executive action and the tone of hearings in Washington for the next two years. That matters on this side of the Pacific because so many familiar names on the Australian stock market now earn, report or price in US dollars. Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX:WDS) Energy Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX:WDS) 31.83 AUD -1.590 4.758% Last Updated at: 2026-11-03T00:26:00Z , the Perth-headquartered oil and gas producer with liquefied natural gas operations spanning Western Australia and North America, is one of the clearest examples of a local business whose fortunes have been tied to geopolitical decisions made far from home.

Midterm elections never attract the wall-to-wall coverage of a presidential campaign, yet their consequences filter through global markets in ways that are easy to underestimate. Control of the House and Senate determines whether an administration can pass its domestic agenda, how budgets are negotiated, and which industries face scrutiny from congressional committees.

Expectations have shifted noticeably in recent months. Control of the lower chamber has long been considered likely to change hands, while the upper chamber was until recently viewed as safely out of reach for the opposition. Several closely watched contests have since been reclassified as genuine toss-ups, including races in states that have not sent an opposition senator to Washington in generations. The practical result is that a divided balance of power now looks more plausible than it did at the start of the year.

Woodside Production Jumps 12% as Scarborough LNG Start Nears
sum: Australian energy giant Woodside Energy reported a sharp rebound in production during the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger liquefied natural gas (LNG) output and improved gas prices, even as the company lowered the upper end of its annual production forecast.

Woodside produced 46.2 million barrels of oil equivalent (MMboe) during the quarter ending September 30, an increase of 12% from the previous quarter. Production was nevertheless 9% below the same period last year.
Quarterly operating revenue reached $4.28 billion, up 2% from the second quarter and 27% year-over-year, reflecting higher LNG sales and stronger realized gas prices.

The company's average realized LNG price climbed 27% quarter-over-quarter to $84 per barrel of oil equivalent, benefiting from stronger international gas markets and LNG trading activities undertaken earlier in the year.
The production recovery was largely driven by the Pluto LNG facility in Western Australia, which resumed higher output following planned maintenance during the second quarter.
Operational reliability remained strong, reaching 99.8% at Pluto LNG, 99.3% at the North West Shelf Project and 99.2% at Senegal's Sangomar oil development.

Despite the quarterly improvement, Woodside narrowed its full-year production forecast to 174 million–181 million barrels of oil equivalent, compared with its previous guidance of 174 million–185 million barrels.

sum: Shares in Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX: WDS) are trading higher after a research report from Macquarie teased the idea of the oil and gas major being a takeover target.
The research report issued on Friday morning argued that the Strait of Hormuz crisis has de-rated Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG) assets for now, and arguably permanently.
Macquarie said this could mean there is more pressure for mergers and acquisitions in the LNG space, "making Woodside a viable target".
The broker is arguing that consolidation in the energy sector will continue, and notes that Exxon Mobil Corp (NYSE: XOM) missed out on buying assets in Guyana 12 months ago.
Quoting Bloomberg as a source, Macquarie writes that ExxonMobil is "screening LNG acquisitions including Woodside".
With US shale consolidations done and opportunities maturing, international deals make sense again, particularly in the LNG segment (post Strait of Hormuz).
Woodside is an attractive candidate, they said, with its M&A strategy over the past five years building a company that aligned strategically with what ExxonMobil would be after.

According to reporting by CNBC, the oil price rose more than 9% yesterday and is up another 2% today.
These gains came after further conflict between the US and Iran regarding the Strait of Hormuz, which is such an important conduit for oil, gas and other commodities the world uses.

Additionally, US President Donald Trump has announced a plan to introduce shipping fees in the Strait of Hormuz and blockage Iran ports again. He said US is the guardian of the oil route and would charge a 20% fee on all cargo shipped.
Energy flow was already disrupted, but with this latest news, it looks like the end of these issues are no longer as close as it seemed.
The Australian energy giant is very leveraged to energy prices. New revenue can largely add to net profit before tax because its costs don’t usually rise in line with revenue.

It’s looking like this fuel situation will remain problematic for even longer than people were hoping, which is bad news for users of fuel, but likely helpful for Woodside’s earnings in the near-term.

With Hormuz closed, is there an opening to buy Woodside shares?
sum: Well, it seems we are back to square one in the Strait of Hormuz. The fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran apparently collapsed over the weekend. The United States has resumed strikes on Iran, while Iran has announced that, once again, ships are not permitted to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Does this mean investors should look to ASX energy shares like Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX: WDS)?

Yes, we seem to be in a new phase of crisis when it comes to this all-important, and now universally recognised global chokepoint. With ships unable to transit the Strait, markets have turned bearish. The S&P/ASX 200 Index (ASX: XJO) is lower today, currently down by about 0.4%. But naturally, ASX energy shares like Woodside are going the other way. Woodside itself is currently up 0.3% in today's session to $29.14 a share. Since last Tuesday, this stock, the largest oil and gas producer on the ASX, has lifted by a confident 4.15%.
Although not quite as high as the near-$36 levels we were seeing back in April, Woodside is still up by more than 23% in 2026 to date. Over the past 12 months, investors have enjoyed a 21% return.
Despite these impressive gains, Wodoside shares are still trading on an eye-catching dividend yield of 5.67% at present.
So, with global oil prices spiking once again, and a yield of that size on the table, are Woodside shares currently in the buy zone?

I think anyone debating this question is missing the forest for the trees. In Warren Buffett's view of investing, which I share, good investing practice involves buying high-quality companies that have the ability to compound their earnings over many years at cheap prices.
I think Woodside falls short on a few of those criteria. Firstly, Woodside shares are becoming more expensive, not cheaper, as a result of recent events. That's not a buy signal in my book.

items.t: Woodside Denies ExxonMobil Takeover Approach as Shares Slide 2.7%
sum: Woodside Energy said on Monday it was not aware of any proposal from ExxonMobil and was not engaged in discussions regarding a potential transaction. The Australian group responded to media speculation fuelled since Friday by a Bloomberg report indicating the US major was considering a takeover of Woodside to deepen its presence in liquefied natural gas (LNG) and Asian markets. "Woodside is not aware of any proposal and confirms it is not in discussions regarding a potential transaction with ExxonMobil Corporation," the company said in a statement issued Monday.

Woodside shares fell 2.7% at the open of the Australian stock exchange on Monday. Oil prices simultaneously dropped 4%, hitting their lowest level since March, after the United States and Iran announced an initial deal to end their conflict and reopen traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. ExxonMobil Australia declined to comment. Australian rival Santos fell a steeper 4.3% in early trade.

On Friday, Woodside's secondary US-listed shares had surged 8.35% following the Bloomberg report. According to those reports, ExxonMobil was seeking to deepen its LNG presence and secure direct access to Asian markets, notably Japan and South Korea. Acquiring Woodside would give the US major a portfolio of operational export infrastructure in Western Australia as well as long-term supply contracts.

Australia's leading LNG exporter, Woodside recently increased its stake in the Browse project to about 42% by pre-empting a sale by PetroChina of its 10.67% share to Inpex. The Browse project is described as Australia's largest undeveloped conventional gas resource. The move consolidates Woodside's operational control over one of its most strategic gas assets, for which a final investment decision has yet to be taken.

According to a sector analysis note, Woodside would have recorded a production high in 2025 of 198.8 million barrels of oil equivalent (MMboe), or around 545,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, with production costs at $7.8/boe.

sum: Threats from US President Donald Trump to strike power plants in Iran prompted a sharp plunge in Australian shares on Monday before the market recovered, ending trade slightly lower after oil prices barely moved following Iran’s vow to retaliate.

Since the start of March, the S&P/ASX 200 has lost more than $300 billion. The index momentarily slipped below $3 trillion on Monday for the first time since May, edging toward a technical correction – a 10 per cent fall from its previous peak – before clawing back some gains to close down 62.5 points, or 0.74 per cent lower, at 8365.9.
The global sell-off in stocks, gold and bonds has deepened as the US and Iran harden their rhetoric and signal a potential escalation to their conflict, which is entering its fourth week.

Trump issued a 48-hour ultimatum to Tehran on Sunday to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — crucial for the flow of oil and gas from the Middle East — failing which the US will “obliterate” Iran’s power plants. The Islamic Republic responded that any such attack would prompt it to shut the waterway indefinitely and target US and Israeli energy infrastructure across the region.

Bonds sold off as the prolonged war threatened to stoke inflation, slow growth and push central banks to consider interest-rate hikes. Futures contracts indicated losses would extend to Europe and the US. Gold slid for a ninth day to around $US4360 an ounce, underscoring the broad-based retreat across assets.

While the reaction in stocks was more pronounced, the response to the latest escalation in rhetoric was more muted in oil markets. Brent was initially volatile before edging down marginally to trade around $111.86 a barrel. Both Brent, the international standard, and US oil WTI have surged more than 70 per cent this year.
The Australian dollar traded lower, around US69.63¢, after the local market closed.

Buying ASX energy shares? Here's how Santos and Woodside shares stacked up in January
sum: Santos Ltd (ASX: STO) and Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX: WDS) shares both raced ahead of the 1.8% gains delivered by the S&P/ASX 200 Index (ASX: XJO) in January. And one stock significantly outperformed the other.
Woodside closed out December trading for $23.59 a share. At market close on 30 January, shares were changing hands for $25.37 apiece. This saw Woodside shares up 7.6% for the month.
Santos shares closed on 31 December at $6.17 each. On 30 January, shares closed the day trading for $7.01 apiece, putting Santos shares up 13.6% for the first month of 2026.
Both ASX 200 energy shares enjoyed a strong uplift in global oil prices over the month.

Spurred by the United States military action in Venezuela and fears of a larger-scale conflict with Iran, the Brent crude oil price soared from US$60.75 per barrel on 2 January to US$70.69 per barrel on 30 January, up 16.4%.
Both ASX 200 energy shares also reported their quarterly results in January.
Woodside shares closed up 2.7% on 28 January following the release of the company's December quarter update.

Here's the earnings forecast out to 2028 for Woodside shares
sum: Owning Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX: WDS) shares can be a volatile ride because of the shifts in energy prices over the months and years as supply and demand shift.
It's challenging to predict what's going to happen next, but analysts can gain insights from certain factors (such as production) and forecast Woodside's revenue and costs.
We're going to look at what experts think of Woodside shares and the profit prospects in the next few years.
The 2025 financial year is already over for Woodside, but investors haven't seen what the numbers are yet, so we're going to look at what analysts think those numbers may be.

UBS is predicting that FY25 could see US$12.8 billion of revenue, US$3.95 billion of operating profit (EBIT) and US$2.2 billion of net profit. The balance sheet is projected to have reached US$7.3 billion of net debt at the end of 2025.
These final projections before the actual result's release in February were in response to the 2025 fourth quarter production.
UBS noted that production was 4% better and revenue was 7% ahead of market expectations due to stronger oil production from both Mad Dog (US Gulf Coast) and Sangomar (Senegal).
